grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Nosotros llevamos, leemos y compartimos. Ustedes llevan, leen y comparten.
grammar.note_en:
Nosotros means “we”: the speaker includes himself or herself in a group. Nosotros llevamos cuatro sillas means “We carry four chairs”. Ustedes means plural “you”, addressing more than one listener. Ustedes tienen la silla negra y tres sillas blancas means “You have the black chair and three white chairs”. The context tells you who is included. Here these words distinguish the organisers, waiting readers and the family using the same courtyard. Ustedes is the normal plural address used in this Mexican setting. This chapter does not introduce another plural address paradigm.

A regular present verb agrees with its subject. For nosotros, an -ar verb takes -amos, an -er verb -emos and an -ir verb -imos: llevamos, leemos, compartimos mean “we carry”, “we read” and “we share”. Compare llevo, leo, comparto from the singular pattern. For ustedes, the corresponding endings are -an, -en and -en: llevan, leen, comparten mean “you carry/read/share” when addressing a group. The same third-person plural forms also describe people being spoken about. Ana y Luis llevan las cuatro sillas means “Ana and Luis carry the four chairs”; Ustedes llevan uses the same verb shape while addressing the listeners. Do not decide between “they” and plural “you” from the ending alone.

The reference table gathers demonstrated forms: nosotros llevamos / ustedes llevan, “we carry / you carry”; nosotros leemos / ustedes leen, “we read / you read”; nosotros abrimos / ustedes abren, “we open / you open”; nosotros compartimos / ustedes comparten, “we share / you share”. Abrir and compartir follow the same -ir pattern. Nosotros esperamos means “We wait”; Nosotros comemos de nueve a diez, “We eat from nine to ten”. The chapter’s plurals refer to genuine groups taking coordinated actions, not to a single respectful listener. Usted remains singular and uses a singular third-person verb, as in chapter 6.

The new numbers are cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez: “five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten”. They name quantities without noun gender changes in these uses: cinco personas, “five people”; cinco sillas, “five chairs”. Ordinal numbers describe position in an order. Primer turno means “first turn”; segundo turno, “second turn”. The citation form primero appears here as primer before the masculine singular noun turno. Only the forms demonstrated in the story are required in this chapter. The new red chair is a separate chair brought from the mother’s house; it does not silently change the cupboard’s established four-chair inventory.

Saturday is sábado and Sunday is domingo. Hoy es sábado means “Today is Saturday”; Mañana es domingo means “Tomorrow is Sunday”. These are days, while a hora is an hour. A las siete means “at seven o’clock”. Son las siete means “It is seven o’clock”. Spanish uses the plural las for these clock hours. El primer turno empieza a las siete y termina a las ocho means “The first turn starts at seven and finishes at eight”. De nueve a diez means “from nine to ten”. The timetable gives consecutive slots, each lasting one hour. The reading does not teach separate morning/evening labels. The dated calendar and clocks are fictional story aids, not a real event schedule.

Llegan cinco personas means “Five people arrive”: llegar concerns reaching a place, not merely being there. Hay diez personas y cuatro sillas; faltan seis sillas means “There are ten people and four chairs; six chairs are missing”. Faltan is plural because the missing chairs are plural. In No faltan libros, “There is no shortage of books”, the books are again plural. Empieza means “starts”; termina means “finishes”. The present empieza has ie in its stem; this chapter uses that demonstrated singular form and does not infer a complete new stem-changing paradigm.

Se sienta means “sits down” for one person; se sientan for several. Luis se sienta en la silla negra means “Luis sits down on the black chair”; cinco personas se sientan means “five people sit down”. Learn these as the two bounded forms supplied here. This is not yet the full reflexive system: do not build other person forms from this example. The final scene contrasts the same reader’s successful reading of large written ocho/nueve with difficulty reading the small sign. The story does not identify that reader as Rosa, diagnose a condition, or equate visual difficulty with inability to understand a text.
